week.t: NASA briefs on Artemis III and the road back to the Moon
AI proves a cousin of the Riemann hypothesis
Perseverance sets the off-world driving record

tiles.cap: A cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice is the world's biggest telescope
tiles.nums: neutrinos through your fingernail every second
tiles.p1: Neutrinos fly straight through planets without noticing. IceCube buried 5,000 light sensors in South Pole ice and waits for the rare one that hits an atom and flashes. It caught neutrinos from black holes billions of light-years away.
tiles.p2: Why now: it won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics on 6 October.
deep: How you see a particle that touches nothing

Neutrinos barely interact, so you need a huge amount of stuff for one to hit. IceCube uses a cubic kilometre of clear ice as the target. When a neutrino finally smacks an atom, it kicks off a charged particle that moves faster than light does in ice and gives off a faint blue glow, which the buried sensors catch.
Why the South Pole

Ice at 1.5 to 2.5 km down is some of the clearest material on Earth, it is already there for free, and it is dark. The sensors were lowered down holes melted with hot water and have been frozen in place since 2010.
What it found

Neutrinos with millions of times the energy of anything our accelerators make, arriving from a flaring galaxy 4 billion light-years away and from our own Milky Way. We can now point at the sky and ask what is firing them, with a messenger nothing can block.
The person
Francis Halzen, 82, born in Belgium, a theorist at the University of Wisconsin who had the idea in the 1980s and spent 30 years getting it built. Physics Nobel 2026, awarded on 6 October.

tiles.cap: A Mars robot just set the off-world driving record. It drove itself.
tiles.p1: Perseverance beat Opportunity's 8-year record in half the time. 90% of it was self-driven: radio to Earth takes up to 20 minutes, so no human can steer live.
tiles.p2: Same problem NASA's Moon-base rovers are being designed around right now.
deep: Why it can't be driven from Earth

A radio signal takes 4 to 20 minutes to reach Mars depending on where the planets are. By the time a driver on Earth saw a rock, the rover would already have hit it. So drives are planned in the morning and the rover executes them alone.
How AutoNav works

While rolling, the rover photographs the ground ahead in stereo, builds a 3D map, scores every patch for danger, picks a path, and repeats, several times a minute. Opportunity could do a crude version about 5% of the time. Perseverance does it 90% of the time and drives up to 412 metres in a day.
The record
45.22 km on 11 October 2026, beating Opportunity's 45.16 km, set over 14 years. Perseverance did it in under six. NASA has extended its mission to the end of 2028.
What it's doing out there
Climbing the rim of Jezero Crater, an ancient lake bed, collecting rock cores in sealed tubes that a future mission is meant to bring back to Earth.

tiles.cap: One warm patch of ocean is rewriting this year's weather
tiles.p1: The 2026 El Niño is the strongest ever measured. It held the Atlantic's first hurricane back until 7 October (a record), while the eastern Pacific had its busiest storm year ever.
tiles.p2: For Singapore, El Niño usually means drier, hazier, warmer seas. Watch and see.
deep: What El Niño actually is

Normally trade winds push warm Pacific water west toward Asia. Every few years the winds weaken and the warm water sloshes back east toward South America. That one shift changes where rain falls across half the planet.
Why the Atlantic went quiet

El Niño strengthens high winds over the Atlantic that shear hurricanes apart before they form. 2026 was so strong that the first hurricane, Isaias, did not appear until 7 October, the latest on record. It still reached Category 3 and hit Florida on 9 October.
And the Pacific went wild
Warmer water east of Mexico fed storm after storm. By mid-October the eastern Pacific had its most energetic season ever measured.
What it means here
El Niño years bring Singapore less rain, more heat and a longer fire season in Sumatra and Kalimantan. That is the haze tile on this wall.

tiles.cap: Pond algae gave scientists a light switch for brain cells
tiles.p1: An alga steers toward light with a protein that opens like a gate under blue light. Put that gene in a neuron, shine a light, the neuron fires on command.
tiles.p2: Memory, fear, sleep and tremors are all being mapped this way. 2026 Nobel in Medicine.
deep: The trick

Neurons fire when charged atoms rush through gates in their membrane. Channelrhodopsin, a protein from a pond alga, is a gate that opens when blue light hits it. Insert its gene into a neuron and you have a cell that fires whenever you flash it.
Who did what

Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel found and decoded the algal protein. Karl Deisseroth, a psychiatrist and engineer at Stanford, got it working in brain cells in 2005 and built the tools to use it in living animals.
Why it's a big deal

Before this you could only stimulate a lump of brain with electricity. Now you can switch one exact type of cell on or off with millisecond timing and watch what changes: a memory, a craving, a tremor.
Already in people
Light-sensitive proteins have been put into the eyes of a blind patient, who regained partial vision. Medicine Nobel 2026, awarded 5 October.

tiles.cap: A five-storey waterfall in Antarctica runs blood red
tiles.p1: Blood Falls is water from a lake sealed under a glacier for ~2 million years, salty and full of iron. It rusts the instant it meets air. Microbes live down there breathing iron, not oxygen.
tiles.p2: Closest thing on Earth to the buried ocean on Jupiter's moon Europa.
deep: Where it comes from

The water seeps out of the Taylor Glacier in Antarctica's Dry Valleys. It started as seawater trapped under the ice around two million years ago, then got concentrated into a brine so salty it stays liquid well below zero.
Why red
The brine is packed with dissolved iron and has had no oxygen for ages. The second it hits air the iron oxidises, the same chemistry as a rusting bike.
Who lives there
Microbes that have been sealed in the dark with no sunlight and no oxygen the whole time. They get energy by shuttling electrons between iron and sulfur compounds.
Why NASA cares
Europa and Enceladus have salty oceans under ice. Blood Falls is the best place on Earth to test whether life can run on that kind of chemistry, and how to detect it.

tiles.cap: An AI proved a cousin of the hardest problem in maths
tiles.p1: The Riemann hypothesis is a 167-year-old question about how primes are spread. On 6 October an AI settled the "quasi-Riemann hypothesis", a softer version, and human experts have checked it.
tiles.p2: Mathematicians are split between "staggering" and "what's left for us?"
deep: The problem
Primes look random, but the Riemann hypothesis says their spacing follows a hidden pattern tied to a function called zeta. Proving it has resisted everyone since 1859 and carries a $1 million prize.
What the AI did

On 6 October OpenAI released hundreds of machine-written papers. One proved the quasi-Riemann hypothesis, a strictly weaker statement that still says a lot about primes. Earlier AI claims had holes; this one has been checked line by line by mathematicians at Stanford and elsewhere and stands.
Why mathematicians are rattled

Some call it the biggest AI-for-maths result so far. Others ask what a mathematician's job is if machines can find and prove deep results. Quanta ran a piece titled 'Is AI the end of math as we know it?'
Your angle
Olympiad-style problems are now routine for these systems. The skills that still matter are choosing which question to ask and knowing when a proof is beautiful rather than merely correct.

tiles.cap: Stare at this and your eyes will invent a colour
tiles.p1: Your three colour sensors tire out separately. Wear out green, look at white, and you see a magenta ghost. That's an afterimage.
tiles.p2: Then mix red, green and blue light yourself in the PhET simulator.
deep: What's happening in your eye

Your retina has three kinds of cone cells, roughly for red, green and blue. Stare at one colour and the cones for it get fatigued and fire less. Look at white, and the other two shout louder, so you see the opposite colour.
The test
Look at the white dot in the green disc for 30 seconds without moving your eyes. Then look at a blank white wall. You should see a magenta disc that follows your gaze and fades over several seconds.
Try variations
Stare at red and you see cyan. Stare at blue and you see yellow. Half-cover the shape and the ghost has a hard edge. Blink and it jumps.
Mix light yourself
Red + green light = yellow. All three = white. Your screen does this with every pixel.

tiles.cap: What a warm sea does to a coral, zoomed to the cell
tiles.p1: Corals are animals that farm algae inside their cells. Heat the water a couple of degrees and the algae turn toxic, so the coral throws them out and goes white.
tiles.p2: Record-warm seas this El Niño year have reef scientists on alert.
deep: Corals are animals

Each coral polyp is a tiny animal related to jellyfish. Inside its cells live algae that photosynthesise and hand over most of the sugar. The coral gets food; the algae get a safe home. That is why reefs grow in clear, sunlit, nutrient-poor water.
What heat does

One to two degrees above normal for a few weeks and the algae's photosynthesis goes haywire, producing toxic by-products. The coral ejects them. Without the algae's colour you see the white skeleton through the clear tissue: bleaching.
Dead or not
A bleached coral is starving, not dead. If the water cools soon it can take algae back in. If heat lasts months, it dies and the reef crumbles.
This year

Record-warm seas during the 2026 El Niño put reefs from the Indian Ocean to the Pacific at risk. Scientists are also finding some corals recover faster when touching healthy neighbours of the same genetics.

tiles.cap: A desert shrub air-conditions its leaves at 50 °C
tiles.p1: Most plants shut their pores in heat and cook. This Death Valley shrub opens up and lets evaporation chill its leaves below air temperature. It sweats.
tiles.p2: Crop scientists are reading its genes to heat-proof wheat and rice.
deep: The gamble

Shutting pores saves water but traps heat; a leaf can cook at 50 °C. This shrub, from Death Valley in California, opens its pores wide and lets water evaporate off the leaf, taking heat with it. Its leaves sit several degrees cooler than the air.
Where the water comes from
Deep roots reach moisture far below the baked surface. The plant spends that water to stay alive on the hottest afternoons of the year.
Why it's being studied now
Heatwaves that models expected in the 2030s are arriving already. Breeders want the genes behind this cooling response to put into wheat and rice.

tiles.cap: Half the universe's ordinary matter was missing. Some just turned up.
tiles.p1: Count every star and gas cloud and you get half the normal matter the Big Bang made. New images show huge faint clouds of hot gas hiding between galaxies.
tiles.p2: Different from dark matter, which may have been glimpsed for the first time on 7 October. Maybe.
deep: Two different mysteries
Ordinary matter is atoms: stars, gas, you. Dark matter is something else we only detect by its gravity, and there is five times more of it. This tile is about the ordinary kind.
The missing half
Measurements of the early universe say how many atoms there should be. Add up everything in galaxies and you get only about half. The rest had to be somewhere.
Found between galaxies

New observations show enormous, thin clouds of hot gas in the spaces between galaxies and along the filaments that connect them. Too faint to see directly before, they hold a big share of the missing atoms.
And dark matter
On 7 October a detector deep underground in South Dakota reported a signal that might be the first direct glimpse of dark matter. One result is not proof. Watch this space.

tiles.cap: Is AI making people dumber? Depends how you use it
tiles.p1: Let it do the thinking and you remember and solve less afterwards. Use it to argue with and check yourself, and you beat people who went without.
tiles.p2: Try: ask an AI to be wrong on purpose, then catch it.
deep: What the studies found

People who had a chatbot write their essay recalled almost nothing of it later. People who used it to question their own draft, or to explain a step they were stuck on, did better than those with no AI at all.
The pattern
Offloading the thinking shrinks the skill. Using the tool as a sparring partner grows it. Same software, opposite results.
Three habits that work
Attempt it first, then ask. Ask it to argue the other side. Ask it to find the mistake in your answer rather than give you one.

tiles.cap: A drowning bee survives by swimming toward the dark
tiles.p1: Bees can't see the shore. But open water glares and the edge is shadowed. Head for the darkest patch and you usually hit land.
tiles.p2: One rule, no map. Robot designers steal tricks like this all the time.
deep: The problem a wet bee has
Water drags its wings down and it cannot take off. It can paddle, but it sits too low to see where the shore is.
The one rule
Open water reflects the bright sky. Banks, reeds and edges are shadowed. Researchers found drenched bees consistently paddle toward the darker side, and in nature that is nearly always land.
Why engineers like it
A single sensor and a single rule solve a problem the animal cannot fully perceive. Swarm robots and cheap drones use the same approach: simple local rules that add up to smart behaviour.

tiles.cap: Could Spider-Man really switch his powers off?
tiles.p1: In the new film Peter builds a superpower inhibitor. Real RNA medicines already mute a single gene without touching DNA. Same idea.
tiles.p2: Connects to the Medicine Nobel: switching biology on and off with precision.
deep: The film
In Spider-Man: Brand New Day, Peter Parker builds a device to switch off new powers he does not want.
The real version

RNA is the working copy of a gene. Medicines called antisense or RNA-interference drugs stick to a specific RNA and stop it being read, muting one gene without changing DNA. They already treat a rare nerve disease and high cholesterol.
Could it work on powers
If a power came from a gene, muting that gene's RNA would dial it down. The catch is delivery: getting the drug into exactly the right cells, which is the hard part of all gene medicine.

tiles.cap: Build a circuit, burn out a bulb, add a dog
tiles.p1: PhET's circuit kit is deliberately silly: wire a battery to a bulb and watch it burn out, or put a dog in the circuit and see if it conducts.
tiles.p2: Then: why NASA's Moon-base rovers run on nuclear modules, not solar. (Lunar night lasts two weeks.)
deep: What to try (coming to this wall as a built-in sim)

Build a loop: battery, wire, bulb. Add a second bulb in the same loop (series) and both dim. Put them on parallel branches and both stay bright. Add a switch. Wire a battery straight to itself and watch it catch fire.
What's really moving
Electrons drift through the wire a few millimetres a second, but they all start moving at once, which is why the bulb lights instantly.
Why Moon rovers go nuclear

Night on the Moon lasts about 14 Earth days and temperatures drop to around minus 170 °C. Solar panels give nothing and batteries freeze. NASA's planned base rovers carry a small nuclear power module for steady heat and electricity through the dark.

tiles.cap: Why the sky over Singapore looks grey this weekend
tiles.p1: Fires on peat in southern Sumatra and Kalimantan make the smoke. All week northeasterly winds pushed it south of us; today they swing southeasterly and the smoke drifts in. Showers should clear it by Sunday.
tiles.p2: The bigger engine behind the dry season: the record El Niño on this wall.
deep: Where the smoke comes from

Farmers and plantations in southern Sumatra and Kalimantan clear land by burning. In a dry year the fires reach peat, compressed ancient plant matter that smoulders underground for weeks and makes thick white smoke.
Why today and not yesterday

All week the wind came from the northeast and east and pushed the smoke south of us. Today it swings southeasterly and brings it in. NEA forecast PSI of 101 to 150 (Unhealthy) for Friday 23 October, after Moderate readings of 71 to 96 on Thursday evening.
What PSI measures
It tracks fine particles 2.5 microns across, about one thirtieth of a hair's width, which go deep into the lungs. Above 100 the advice is to cut outdoor exercise; above 200 to stay in.
When it clears
Showers are forecast and winds turn more southerly over the weekend, so Sunday should be better. The dry season behind it is driven by the record El Niño.

tiles.cap: NUS wove a touchscreen into a sleeve. It goes in the wash.
tiles.p1: Each fibre carries 96 LEDs and senses touch at the same time. Over 5,000 chips are linked by 20,000+ connections, all pulled through a thermal drawing process like making glass fibre. Published in Nature on 22 October.
tiles.p2: First use: a sleeve that shows your body temperature. Led by Asst Prof Tural Khudiyev.
deep: How you make a glowing thread

Start with a thick rod containing the LEDs and wires, heat it, and pull it into a long thin fibre, the same thermal drawing used to make fibre-optic cable. Each fibre ends up with 96 tiny LEDs along it and can sense a fingertip.
Then weave it
54 of those fibres go into ordinary fabric to make a 96 by 54 pixel screen, 168 by 105 mm, on a sleeve. Over 5,000 chips, more than 20,000 connections, and it survives the washing machine.
What it's for

Clothing that shows your temperature or heart rate, or acts as a controller for your phone, without a separate device. Led by Assistant Professor Tural Khudiyev at NUS; published in Nature on 22 October 2026.

tiles.cap: Singapore is sending an AI into orbit the size of a shoebox
tiles.p1: Singapore's space programme is building three satellites to launch in 2026, 2027 and 2028. One runs small AI models in orbit so it sends down answers, not raw photos, and tests perovskite solar cells in space for the first time.
tiles.p2: Another carries a Singapore-built electric engine that can raise or lower a satellite's orbit.
deep: The plan
Singapore's Office for Space Technology and Industry is funding three satellites, one launch a year in 2026, 2027 and 2028, built with NTU and local companies.
Satellite one

A 3-unit cubesat, 30 by 10 by 10 cm, that runs small AI models on board to analyse its own photos in orbit and only sends down the useful parts. It also carries perovskite solar cells, a cheaper, lighter kind never before tested in space.
Satellite two

A 16-unit, 30 kg craft with an electric engine from NTU spin-off Aliena that can raise or lower its orbit, plus a detector for atomic oxygen, the corrosive gas that eats spacecraft in very low orbits.
Satellite three
A camera from LightHaus Photonics, tested on the International Space Station, built to pick out objects about a metre across from orbit.
